```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using MatrixCommunityModels
using LinearAlgebra, Printf
using Plots
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
```

## Three genera after a disaster

Between 2006 and 2010 an outbreak of the crown-of-thorns seastar, followed by Cyclone Oli,
reduced the coral cover of the fore reefs of Mo'orea, French Polynesia, from more than 40%
to less than 1%. Kayal et al. (2018) followed the recovery on four reefs of the Mo'orea
Coral Reef Long Term Ecological Research site (LTER 1 and 2 on the north shore, LTER 4 on
the east, LTER 5 on the west). They counted recruits, and tagged and remeasured colonies of
the three genera that build most of the reef: *Acropora*, *Pocillopora* and *Porites*. From
these data they built an integral projection model (IPM) for each genus on each reef.
Colonies are structured by size, and recruits arrive from the plankton in numbers set by
local crowding, so each population is open.

The genera interact only through recruitment. In Mo'orea, recruitment of *Pocillopora*
falls as the coral assemblage grows, whatever its composition; that of *Acropora* rises
with the abundance of *Acropora*; that of *Porites* barely changes (Kayal et al. 2015).
Survival and growth depend on size alone. In this package each genus is a projection net,
and the quantities recruitment reads are pools.

This vignette rebuilds the model from the paper's Appendix S3 and Table S1. It checks the
model against the authors' own kernel functions, run in R, and against the simulations
the paper publishes in its figures.

## Size and the kernels

Size is $z = \log_{10}(S + 1)$, with $S$ the surface area of a colony's living tissue in
cm², on $[0, 7]$ in 100 cells (Appendix S3). From one year to the next a colony of size
$z$ survives with probability $\mathrm{logit}^{-1}(s_0 + s_z z)$. If it survives, its new
size is normal with mean $G_0 + G_z z$ and standard deviation $G_{SD}$. The parameters
differ by genus and reef (Table S1):

```{julia}
taxa = (:acropora, :pocillopora, :porites)
reefs = (:lter1, :lter2, :lter4, :lter5)
label = Dict(:acropora => "Acropora", :pocillopora => "Pocillopora", :porites => "Porites")
println("reef    genus          s0      sz      G0      Gz     GSD      R0       Rγ")
for r in reefs, t in taxa
    p = CORAL_PARAMETERS[r][t]
    @printf("%-6s  %-12s %6.3f  %6.3f  %6.3f  %6.3f  %6.3f  %6.3f  %7.3f\n", r, label[t], p.survival.intercept,
            p.survival.slope, p.growth.intercept, p.growth.slope, p.growth.sd, p.recruitment.intercept, p.recruitment.slope)
end
```

## Recruitment and its reading

Each year $r$ recruits arrive, with sizes normal with mean 0.6 and standard deviation 0.2
(about 3 cm² of tissue, 2 cm across). The paper writes the number as

$$\log r = R_0 + R_\gamma\,\gamma ,$$

where the crowding $\gamma$ is the number of colonies of the genus itself for *Acropora* and
*Porites*, and the summed sizes $z$ of the colonies of all three genera for *Pocillopora*
(Appendix S3, equations iii to v). $R_0$ comes from the recruits counted in 2011-2012 and
$R_\gamma$ from an earlier study. Recruitment is capped at 348 colonies per 10 m² a year,
and a model step is a year on 10 m² of reef.

The units of this equation are not stated. The authors' R script uses the natural
logarithm, and its density and summed sizes are per 10 m², the area of a model iteration.
This is the package's default (`reading = :as_written`), since it is what the authors'
code does. Read that way, the model does not give the published simulations: *Acropora*
and *Porites* end up with several times the share of the assemblage that the paper shows.
A reading that does reproduce them is offered as `reading = :calibrated`, and the
comparisons with the published figures below use it:

- the logarithm is to base 10;
- $R_0$ is for the 25 m² plots in which recruits were counted, so that the recruits per
  10 m² are $0.4 \times 10^{R_0 + R_\gamma \gamma}$;
- $\gamma$ is per m².

This reading was found by trying the natural and base-10 logarithm with recruits and
crowding per m², per 10 m² and per 25 m², against the figures below. It is a
reconstruction, not something the paper states. `coral_recruits` gives the number of
recruits in either reading:

```{julia}
for t in taxa
    @printf("%-12s  at γ = 0: calibrated %6.1f, as written %5.1f recruits per 10 m² (LTER 1)\n", label[t],
            coral_recruits(t, 0.0; reading = :calibrated), coral_recruits(t, 0.0))
end
```

## The genera as nets

`coral` builds one genus on one reef. It is written in this form (abridged from
`src/corals.jl`):

```julia
colony = coral_stage()                                   # z on [0, 7], 100 cells
life = kernel_net(colony, :growing => (y, x) -> survival(x) * growth(y, x))
net = inflow(life, (cell => ctx -> share[i] * recruits(ctx) for (i, cell) in enumerate(stage_names(colony)))...)
species(taxon, net; occupies = [:<taxon>_colonies => trait_weights(colony, z -> 1.0),
                                :<taxon>_log_size => trait_weights(colony, z -> z)],
        reads = ...)                                     # Pocillopora reads the other two log-size pools
```

The recruits are inflows: they do not come from the colonies of the net, so the net has no
births. `share[i]` is the probability that a recruit lands in cell `i`. The genus adds its
colonies and their summed sizes to two pools. *Acropora* and *Porites* read their own
colonies. *Pocillopora* reads the summed sizes of all three. `coral_community` composes
the three genera:

```{julia}
c = coral_community(:lter1; reading = :calibrated)
(species = species_names(c), pools = pool_names(c), states = length(c))
```

## Recovery from an empty reef

The paper's first simulations start from empty reef and let it fill by recruitment alone.
The first recruits arrive in the first step (2010), so 2013, "after 3 years of reef
recovery", is the fourth step and 2015 the sixth. (Four cohorts are visible in the
published size distributions for 2013, and with four steps the elasticities to survival
and growth match those published; see below.)

```{julia}
function recovery(reef; reading = :calibrated, steps = 6)
    c = coral_community(reef; reading)
    return c, project(c, zeros(length(c)), fill(nothing, steps))
end
z = meshpoints(coral_stage())
area = 10 .^ z .- 1
panels = map(reefs) do r
    c, sol = recovery(r)
    p = plot(; xscale = :log10, xlims = (0.1, 1e5), ylims = (0, 60), title = uppercase(String(r)), legend = r === :lter1 ? :topleft : false,
             xlabel = r in (:lter4, :lter5) ? "Colony area (cm²)" : "", ylabel = r in (:lter1, :lter4) ? "Colonies per 10 m² per cell" : "")
    stacked = zeros(length(z))
    for (t, colour) in zip(taxa, (:blue, :red, :green))
        lower = copy(stacked)
        stacked .+= sol[t][5, :]
        plot!(p, area[2:end], stacked[2:end]; fillrange = lower[2:end], color = colour, alpha = 0.7, lw = 0, label = label[t])
    end
    p
end
plot(panels...; layout = (2, 2), size = (800, 560))
```

These are the predicted assemblages of 2013, drawn as in Fig. 3a-d of the paper: colonies
in each mesh cell, stacked by genus. *Pocillopora* dominates everywhere, as published. The
cohorts are clearer here than in the paper, where the youngest cohorts are smaller (see
"Where the model and its sources part").

The paper prints the share of each genus in the summed sizes of the assemblage on each
panel of Fig. 3 (2013) and Fig. S4 (2015). Fig. S2 gives the colonies per 10 m² of each
genus in 2013, read here from the bar chart to the nearest few colonies.

```{julia}
shares(c, n) = (p = pool_totals(c, n, nothing); x = [getproperty(p, Symbol(t, :_log_size)) for t in taxa]; 100 .* x ./ sum(x))
colonies(c, n) = (p = pool_totals(c, n, nothing); [getproperty(p, Symbol(t, :_colonies)) for t in taxa])
fig3 = Dict(:lter1 => [3, 96, 2], :lter2 => [2, 97, 1], :lter4 => [6, 93, 1], :lter5 => [2, 95, 3])
figS4 = Dict(:lter1 => [4, 93, 3], :lter2 => [3, 96, 1], :lter4 => [6, 93, 0], :lter5 => [2, 94, 4])
figS2 = Dict(:lter1 => [24, 612, 14], :lter2 => [16, 428, 4], :lter4 => [8, 82, 4], :lter5 => [4, 128, 8])
fmt(v) = join([@sprintf("%3.0f", x) for x in v], " ")
println("            share 2013 (%)            share 2015 (%)            colonies 2013 (per 10 m²)")
println("reef        here        paper         here        paper         here             paper (Fig. S2)")
for r in reefs
    c, sol = recovery(r)
    @printf("%-6s  %s   %s     %s   %s     %s   %s\n", r, fmt(shares(c, sol.u[5, :])), fmt(fig3[r]),
            fmt(shares(c, sol.u[7, :])), fmt(figS4[r]), join([@sprintf("%4.0f", x) for x in colonies(c, sol.u[5, :])], " "), fmt(figS2[r]))
end
```

Every share of 2013 is within a percentage point of the published one (allowing for the
rounding of both), and every share of 2015 within three. The colonies of *Pocillopora* are
within a quarter of Fig. S2. Read as written, the same model gives this:

```{julia}
println("reef    share 2013 as written (%)   colonies 2013 as written")
for r in reefs
    c, sol = recovery(r; reading = :as_written)
    @printf("%-6s  %s                 %s\n", r, fmt(shares(c, sol.u[5, :])), join([@sprintf("%5.1f", x) for x in colonies(c, sol.u[5, :])], " "))
end
```

*Pocillopora* holds 19 to 24 percentage points less of the assemblage than published, and
its colonies number in the tens, not the hundreds of Fig. S2.

## Elasticities

Table S2 of the paper lists the elasticity of each population's predicted change in summed
size over 2010-2013 to each parameter. Its R script (section 4) computes the elasticity of
the ratio of the summed size in the last year to that in the first, `surf[[6]]/surf[[1]]`
for five years. Here the ratio is that of the fourth step to the first, and the derivatives
are central differences. Shown for LTER 1:

```{julia}
function surface_ratio(reef, taxon, field, which, factor; reading = :calibrated)
    P = CORAL_PARAMETERS
    sizes = NamedTuple{taxa}(Tuple(t === taxon && field === :recruit_size ?
        (which === :mean ? (0.6 * factor, 0.2) : (0.6, 0.2 * factor)) : (0.6, 0.2) for t in taxa))
    pars = P
    if field !== :recruit_size
        p = P[reef][taxon]
        rate = merge(getproperty(p, field), NamedTuple{(which,)}((getproperty(getproperty(p, field), which) * factor,)))
        pars = merge(P, NamedTuple{(reef,)}((merge(P[reef], NamedTuple{(taxon,)}((merge(p, NamedTuple{(field,)}((rate,))),))),)))
    end
    c = coral_community(reef; parameters = pars, recruit_size = sizes, reading)
    u = project(c, zeros(length(c)), fill(nothing, 4)).u
    s(n) = getproperty(pool_totals(c, n, nothing), Symbol(taxon, :_log_size))
    return s(u[end, :]) / s(u[2, :])
end
elasticity(args...; kw...) = abs((surface_ratio(args..., 1 + 1e-4; kw...) - surface_ratio(args..., 1 - 1e-4; kw...)) /
                                 (2e-4 * surface_ratio(args..., 1.0; kw...)))
items = [(:survival, :intercept), (:survival, :slope), (:growth, :intercept), (:growth, :slope), (:growth, :sd),
         (:recruitment, :intercept), (:recruitment, :slope), (:recruit_size, :mean), (:recruit_size, :sd)]
table_s2 = [0.24 0.31 0.11; 0.02 0.05 0.19; 0.82 0.78 0.82; 0.24 0.79 0.57; 0.00 0.00 0.00;
            0.44 1.56 0.02; 0.29 0.28 0.01; 0.78 0.99 0.61; 0.02 0.01 0.02]      # Table S2, LTER 1
println("parameter                    here (Acr Poc Por)    Table S2 (Acr Poc Por)")
for (i, (f, w)) in enumerate(items)
    e = [elasticity(:lter1, t, f, w) for t in taxa]
    @printf("%-12s %-10s      %5.2f %5.2f %5.2f        %5.2f %5.2f %5.2f\n", f, w, e..., table_s2[i, :]...)
end
```

Survival, growth and the size of recruits match Table S2 closely, here and on the other
three reefs (a check outside this vignette). The elasticities to the intercept and slope
of recruitment do not: they are three to seven times smaller here, and smaller still for
*Pocillopora* when read as written. None of the 54 combinations of logarithm and units
tried (natural or base 10; $R_0$, and the crowding of each kind, per m², 10 m² or 25 m²)
reproduces them (a check outside this vignette). The published model is more sensitive to
recruitment than this one.

## The check against the authors' R code

The authors' script (Kayal 2017) is a template. It fits its models to a data file it does
not name, and its recruitment functions call objects that do not exist, so it does not run
as it stands. `test/reference/R/run_coral_reference.R` reads the script at run time. It
evaluates only its survival, growth, kernel and recruit-size functions, with the values of
Table S1, and writes the recruitment of Appendix S3 in both readings. The kernels and 40
years of recovery on every reef, in both readings, agree with this package to rounding:

```{julia}
reference(file) = [split(l, ",") for l in readlines(joinpath(pkgdir(MatrixCommunityModels), "test", "reference", file))[2:end]]
codes = Dict("Acr" => :acropora, "Poc" => :pocillopora, "Por" => :porites)
reef_of = Dict("1" => :lter1, "2" => :lter2, "4" => :lter4, "5" => :lter5)
rows = reference("coral_runs.csv")
worst = 0.0
for reading in (:calibrated, :as_written), (code, r) in reef_of
    c, sol = recovery(r; reading, steps = 40)
    for row in rows
        (row[1] == String(reading) && row[2] == code) || continue
        p = pool_totals(c, sol.u[parse(Int, row[3]) + 1, :], nothing)
        theirs = parse(Float64, row[5])
        theirs > 0 && (global worst = max(worst, abs(getproperty(p, Symbol(codes[row[4]], :_colonies)) / theirs - 1)))
    end
end
(largest_relative_difference_in_colonies = worst,)
```

## After 2015

The paper projects to 2020 from the assemblages observed in 2015. Those data are not used
here, so the projection below continues the recovery from empty reef, for 40 years
(*Acropora* blue, *Pocillopora* red, *Porites* green). Recruitment of *Acropora* rises with
its own density, with nothing to stop it but the cap.

```{julia}
plot(; layout = (1, 4), size = (900, 260), legend = false)
for (j, r) in enumerate(reefs)
    c, sol = recovery(r; steps = 40)
    p = reduce(vcat, permutedims(colonies(c, row)) for row in eachrow(sol.u))
    for (k, colour) in enumerate((:blue, :red, :green))
        plot!(2009 .+ (0:40), p[:, k]; subplot = j, color = colour, lw = 2, yscale = :log10, ylims = (1, 1e4),
              title = uppercase(String(r)), xlabel = "Year", ylabel = j == 1 ? "Colonies per 10 m²" : "")
    end
end
plot!()
```

```{julia}
for r in reefs
    c, sol = recovery(r; steps = 40)
    capped = findfirst(row -> coral_recruits(:acropora, pool_totals(c, row, nothing).acropora_colonies; reef = r, reading = :calibrated) >= CORAL_RECRUITMENT_CAP,
                       collect(eachrow(sol.u)))
    @printf("%-6s Acropora recruitment reaches the cap of 348 in %s; colonies in 2049: %s\n", r,
            capped === nothing ? "none of these years" : string(2009 + capped - 1), fmt(colonies(c, sol.u[end, :])))
end
```

*Pocillopora* levels off within a decade, held by its own density dependence. *Acropora*
keeps increasing on the north shore (LTER 1 and 2) and the east (LTER 4), fastest at
LTER 1, but from an empty reef it does not reach the cap within 40 years. Kayal et al.
(2018) report that only *Acropora* on the north shore reached the cap, in their
projections to 2020; those started from the larger *Acropora* populations observed in 2015
and with larger *Acropora* recruits (1.2 rather than 0.6), and cannot be repeated here.
Without the cap the positive feedback of *Acropora* on its own recruitment has no limit;
the cap is part of the model, not of the reef.

## The comparison with the authors' code and the paper

| Check | Agreement |
|---|---|
| Survival-growth kernels against the authors' `P_z1z` functions, 12 populations | absolute difference below 1e-12 |
| Recovery from empty reef, 40 years, four reefs, both readings, against the R reference | relative difference below 1e-14 |
| Share of each genus in the summed sizes in 2013 (Fig. 3a-d), 12 values | within 1 percentage point |
| Share of each genus in 2015 (Fig. S4a-d), 12 values | within 3 percentage points |
| Colonies of *Pocillopora* per 10 m² in 2013 (Fig. S2a, read from the figure) | within 22% |
| Colonies of *Acropora* and *Porites* in 2013 (Fig. S2a; published values 4 to 24) | within 10 colonies, mostly fewer |
| Elasticities to survival, growth and recruit size (Table S2, LTER 1) | within 0.05, except *Pocillopora* growth slope and recruit mean size (0.68 against 0.79; 0.78 against 0.99) |
| Elasticities to the intercept and slope of recruitment (Table S2) | no: three to seven times smaller |
| Shape of the size distributions in 2013 (Fig. 3a-d) | in part: the cohorts are where published, but the youngest are too large |
| The recruitment cap reached only by north-shore *Acropora*, by 2020 (Appendix S3) | not tested: those runs start from data not used here |

## What is measured and what is assumed

| Quantity | Source |
|---|---|
| Survival and growth by size, by genus and reef | fitted to colonies tagged in 2011-2013 (Table S1) |
| Recruitment intercept $R_0$, by genus and reef | fitted to recruits counted in 2011-2012 (Table S1) |
| Recruitment slope $R_\gamma$, by genus | from Kayal et al. (2015), not read here (Table S1) |
| What recruitment responds to: own density, or summed sizes of the assemblage | Appendix S3 |
| Size of recruits, mean 0.6 and sd 0.2 | Appendix S3 (the paper's initial runs; 1.2 and 0.4 for *Acropora* in its later runs, available as `recruit_size`) |
| Cap of 348 recruits per 10 m² a year | Appendix S3 |
| Mesh: $z$ on $[0, 7]$ in 100 cells | Appendix S3 |
| Base-10 logarithm, $R_0$ per 25 m², $\gamma$ per m² | calibrated here against Fig. 3, Fig. S2 and Fig. S4; not stated in the paper |
| Start: empty reef, first recruits in the first step | the paper's initial runs; the step count chosen to match Fig. 3 and Table S2 |

## Where the model and its sources part

- The units of the recruitment equation are a reconstruction. The package's default
  follows the authors' script; the calibrated reading used for the comparisons here
  reproduces the published shares of the assemblage (Fig. 3, Fig. S4) and, roughly, the
  densities (Fig. S2). It does not reproduce the shape of the published size
  distributions: in Fig. 3a the youngest cohorts of *Pocillopora* are about a fifth of the
  oldest, while here they are about as large. Nor does it reproduce the elasticities to
  recruitment of Table S2, which are three to seven times larger than here. Both point to a
  stronger density dependence of *Pocillopora* recruitment in the published model than in
  any reading tried. A reading with stronger density dependence (crowding per 10 m²)
  matches the cohort shapes better and the shares and densities worse. The paper's own
  code, which would settle the question, is not published in runnable form.
- The authors' R script, read as written, does not run (see above), and in its
  recruitment of *Pocillopora* it reads `m.parPoc["recr.Intercep"]`, a misspelt name that
  gives `NA` in R. The script uses the natural logarithm, which the published figures rule
  out.
- The crowding of *Pocillopora* is the sum of the sizes $z$ (logarithms of area) of the
  colonies, as Appendix S3 writes it and Fig. S2b labels it ("sum log-sizes"), not their
  summed area.
- The paper's updated runs start from the assemblages observed in 2013 and 2015 (MCR LTER
  data on the Environmental Data Initiative). Those data were not used, so Fig. 4, Fig. S5
  to S8, Tables S3 and S4 and the projections to 2020 are not reproduced.
- Values read from the figures (Fig. S2) are approximate, to a few colonies.

## Sources

Read in full: the paper (the authors' accepted manuscript on eScholarship, which carries
the DOI 10.1111/ele.13153) and its Supporting Information (Appendices S1 to S3, Figs. S1 to
S11, Tables S1 to S4), and the authors' R script (GitHub, commit af547a8, no licence).
The publisher's pages refused automated access, so the version of record itself was not
read. Two DOIs carry this paper's title and authors: 10.1111/ele.13153 (*Ecology Letters*
21(12), 1790-1799, online 11 September 2018) and 10.1111/ele.13203 (22(4), 605-615, online
3 February 2019). Crossref and PubMed list both, with the same abstract and no notice
linking them. The eScholarship record, the MCR LTER bibliography and HAL give the first,
which is cited here. Kayal et al. (2015), the source of the recruitment slopes, was not
read. The parameters are the published values of Table S1, typed into
`data/corals/kayal2018_table_s1.csv`; no file of the authors is included in this package.
